title: BOOK TWO. On the end of man as citizen of God's kingdom — the absolutely highest and last end, or eternal beatitude. CHAPTER ONE. Whether there is some highest good of man, and that eternal, and what it is
english: BOOK TWO. On the end of man, as a citizen of God's kingdom — the absolutely highest and last end, or eternal beatitude.
CHAPTER ONE. Whether there is some highest good of man, and that eternal, and what it is.

The common part of sacred theology pursues three things: the absolutely highest and last end of man, namely eternal beatitude; the subject, that is, man himself as a citizen of God; and the principles on which eternal salvation depends, together with the means by which he is directed to it.

title: II. Man's absolutely highest and last end and good is given, and that eternal; Augustine on eternal beatitude
english: II. But for man — the noblest creature and a citizen of God's kingdom — an absolutely highest and last end and good is given, by which he is perfected in every way, and that eternal, which embraces all things to be wished for, as Augustine teaches in book 4 of the City of God, chapter 21.
And in the same sense eternal beatitude, or the possession of the highest and most perfect good, is so called.

title: Every thing has its end; whatever acts tends to some good; intelligent and non-intelligent agents
english: For among all the saints — indeed among the sane — it is confessed that to each thing some end of its own belongs, its own good, and its own perfection: because neither God nor nature does or produces anything in vain, but all things are for an end ([[Genesis 1:31>>Gen. 1:31]]; [[Proverbs 16:4>>Prov. 16:4]]).
2. Whatever acts, whether it works with cognition or without cognition properly so called, acts toward an end, and therefore seeks some goodthat cannot be an end which has no account of good.

3. Although there is a difference — that those which understand move themselves to the end and act by knowing the end and the means, comparing them with one another and ordering these to that end, while those which do not understand are moved rather by natural inclination — yet both act for an end, or, to speak more clearly, tend into an end.

title: 4–5. Perfection and beatitude when the end is attained; the highest good defined as last and most perfect
english: 4. Each thing, if it attains its good and end, is perfect — or, if its nature is intelligent, blessed. For no animal that lacks knowledge can be blessed, and it does not fall to things without reason to be blessed, as Augustine teaches in the book of eighty-three questions, question 1; but on the contrary it is imperfect, wretched, and unhappy if it falls from and is deprived of its end and good.

5. The highest good is called also the last, because it is subjected to no other as a means, or is not at all ordered to the attaining of something higher and greater; and most perfect, because it excludes every defect and need, and gives itself to the one who has it so that it may be perfectly well with him.

title: III–IV. Perfection must be proportioned to the subject; mortal and eternal goods
english: III. But this perfection of the thing that is perfected is necessarily proportioned, so that it cannot be lesser or worse than the thing to be perfected.
For it would not be perfection if it could not perfect its subject — or, what amounts to the same, actuate and exhaust that potency which it has toward perfection, and sufficiently fill its appetite.

IV. Hence it is that to mortal and fleeting things mortal and fleeting perfections also belong, which affect and perfect them as long as they last; but if any thing is eternal and immortal, its good too is eternal and immortal.

For it would be absurd if the perfection of an eternal and immortal thing were placed in something that is by its nature fragile, flowing, and liable to ruin, among those things that are below the first heaven.

title: Dionysius the Carthusian against Scotus; Richard on philosophers; Thomas on duplex contemplation of God
english: Dionysius the Carthusian speaks aptly against Scotus: There is not, he says, the same mode of receiving a natural and acquired form and habit as a supernatural and infused form and habit; nor is the inclination of the created mind to a supernatural form and habit judged natural, but rather supernatural — that is, fitting to a power beyond and above the grade, measure, and limit of its natural condition, namely by respect to a supernatural end. Indeed if it consisted as natural, it could be completed and actuated by a natural cause.

And Richard, whom they call the solid Doctor, holds that philosophers, however excellent in talent, who have not been supernaturally illuminated, have never known nor been able to know true and full beatitude. These are signs of the evangelical light, which in the midst of the darkness of the papacy was not wholly obscured among all.
But also Thomas, whose authority even the scholastic crowd prefers to Scotus: All, he says, who have sensed rightly have placed the end of human life in the contemplation of God.

But the contemplation of God is twofold: one through creatures, which is imperfect, inasmuch as the creature is an effect not proportioned to the Creator but infinitely distant from him. Therefore it leads into an imperfect knowledge of God, in which the philosopher places contemplative happiness — which happiness is nevertheless a way, and to it the whole of philosophical cognition is ordered, proceeding from reasons and considerations of creatures.

The other is the contemplation of God by which he is seen immediately through his essence: this is perfect contemplation, and it is had in the homeland, and is possible for man according to the supposition of faith; whence those things that are toward the end must be proportioned to the end, so that man in the state of the way may be led by the hand to that beatitude not by cognition taken from creatures but by cognition inspired from divine light. And this is the doctrine of theology, whose office it is to command all other sciences and to use them in its service.

title: Why supernatural theology is necessary; five hypotheses before the highest good can be taught
english: So Thomas. From which it is gathered at once what and why this supernatural doctrine and theology is necessary for man beside and beyond the natural sciences: namely because it raises and directs his true practice — which is according to piety — above nature to his highest end and to the good of eternal joy and glory.

That good cannot be taught clearly enough unless other hypotheses have already been settled in the reader's mind, namely: first, the immortality of the rational soul; second, the state of the same when separated from its body; third, the end of this world; fourth, the resurrection of the flesh; fifth, the last judgment.
When these are rightly established, the highest beatitude of God's kingdom, and of man as citizen of this kingdom, will be explained somewhat more solidly.

title: V. The good suited to the rational immortal soul; proof that man has a rational soul
english: V. Since therefore man is endowed with a rational soul, which is immaterial, indissoluble, and immortal, such a good suits him as exceeds the measure and duration of the body and endures with the immortal soul itself after departure from the body: when he has obtained it he will be happy and blessed; but if he falls from it he will be extremely wretched.

Man has a rational soul: this is confessed among all, and we all experience it from the operations of the soul in us. For we understand that we arrive from known things at knowledge of unknowns, which is to reason.

From which we gather that there is in us some principle from which this operation flows. This is the soul, which from so excellent an effect we call rational; concerning its nature the following rules are to be observed here in passing.

title: 1. The rational soul is the true informing form of man — not accidental motion, crasis, or Averroist assistance
english: 1. The rational soul is the true form of man.

I mean a form that is not accidental — such as continuous and perennial motion, which Cicero in the first Tusculan Questions believed Aristotle meant by the word entelechyyy, and such as the mixture of the primary qualities, which both impious heretics (Carpocrates, Epiphanes, Prodicus, the Cainites and Antitactae, in Theodoret, book 5 On divine decrees, chapter on man) and Galen (in the book That the manners of the soul follow the temperament of the body, chapters 3 and 4, and Epidemic book 6, and book 3 On affected places) imagined as the form of man;

nor an assisting form, such as Averroes (On the soul book 3, chapter 5) thought to be one for all, in reality separated from all, and joined to individuals only through images of phantasy residing in them;
but an informing form, which informs the body and with it constitutes man in a certain species of things.

title: 2–3. The soul is spiritual and separable from matter; VI hypotheses for teaching the highest good
english: 2. It is of a spiritual nature. This is shown first by its operations, which are far nobler than those that can proceed from a corporeal thing; second by all the places of Holy Scripture that call the rational soul a spirit — as [[Ecclesiastes 12:7>>Eccl. 12:7]]; [[Isaiah 26:9>>Esa. 26:9]]; [[Matthew 27:50>>Matth. 27:50]]; [[Luke 23:46>>Luc. 23:46]]; [[Job 19:30>>Job. 19:30]]; [[Acts 7:60>>Act. 7:60]]; [[1 Corinthians 2:11>>1 Cor. 2:11]] and [[1 Corinthians 6:20>>1 Cor. 6:20]]; [[2 Corinthians 7:1>>2 Cor. 7:1]]; and [[Hebrews 12:9>>Heb. 12:9]].

Against John, bishop of Thessalonica, who in the pseudo-synod of Nicaea, at the beginning of the fifth action, does not fear to say, for establishing the cult of images, that the Catholic Church believes every soul to be corporeal — with many philosophers of the Stoic and Italic sects, with Tertullian and a certain Apollinaris of Alexandria (of whom in the Tripartite History book 5, chapter 44), and according to some with the Luciferians (Augustine, On heresies, chapter 81).

Against all of whom the third Council of Constantinople, or sixth ecumenical, sensed more holy in its eleventh action: God is born, it says, with a human body and likewise with the habit of having a rational and incorporeal soul.
3. It is separable from matter. For experience teaches that all die. But death is nothing other than the separation of the soul from the body.

VI. But here especially is to be considered the immortality of the rational soul, the state of its separation from the body, the resurrection of the flesh, and what follows upon this. For until these are surveyed and set beyond the cast of doubt, the highest good of man and eternal beatitude cannot be taught fully enough and distinctly.

title: VII. Immortality of the soul defined; Bernard, Nyssenus, Augustine, Ambrose on death as change — Cap. 1 close
english: VII. The immortality of the soul is that perfection of it by which, without destruction of its substance, by the kindness of its Creator, it endures forever.

This is opposed to death strictly taken, inasmuch as it is extinction with respect to the destruction of substance. Otherwise certain of the fathers take death more loosely, for  change with respect to its state, whatever that finally is. So Bernard: Every change, he says, is a death. And therefore Nyssenus proves that death is implicated in this life, because this life is subject to change.

Augustine agrees in book 3 against Maximinus the Arian bishop, chapter 12, column 730: Immortality, he says, God alone is said to have, because he alone is immutable. For in every changeable nature the change itself is some death, because it makes something in it not to be what it was. Accordingly the human soul itself, which is therefore called immortal because in whatever way, according to its own mode, it never ceases to live, nevertheless has according to that same mode a certain death of its own: because if it was living justly and sins, it dies to justice; if it was a sinner and is justified, it dies to sin — not to mention its other changes, about which it is long to dispute.

Ambrose agrees in book 3 On faith, chapter 2: And the soul, he says, dies. For the soul that has sinned, it itself shall die. Every rational creature receives accidents and is subject to judgment. But in accidents both the penalty of judgment is corruption and also progress.
